blocks.text: The Werewolf aesthetic is an aesthetic closely tied to the way lycanthropy is used as a metaphor in popular media. The Werewolf character often is used to portray the darker side of humanity -- unrestrained, uncontrollable, filled with unbridled rage and lust -- as well as a metaphor for puberty -- mood swings, physical changes out of one's control, hunger, and a cycle closely tied to the moon. Visually, this manifests as typical horror imagery (blood, sharp teeth, dark foggy nights) combined with some key fashion aspects that have become typical to the modern werewolf trope.

Werewolves have been the subject of stories and folklore for centuries. The first common metaphor you'll encounter is 'werewolf as a metaphor for the Id,' -- the dark, inner self one must suppress; the primal, aggressive nature everyone fights against; the "beast within." This version of the werewolf metaphor shows up everywhere, from film (The Wolf Man, 1941), to television (Oz in Buffy the Vampire Slayer), to video games (The Wolf Among Us, 2013); this metaphor exists even across time, from the earliest depictions of werewolves in media (The Werewolf of Paris, 1933) to modern day. Through this metaphor, you'll find werewolves depicted as bloodthirsty and wild, unable to contain themselves, and at the whim of their emotions and desires.

'Werewolf as a metaphor for puberty' is a relatively newer take, with the oldest example (I Was a Teenage Werewolf, 1957) setting the tone for the other examples to come. This version of the werewolf metaphor takes all the body horror of lycanthropy -- uncontrollable changes, growing hair, getting taller -- and uses it as an apt one-to-one metaphor for puberty. Through this version, you'll find teenage characters struggling with the reality of what they've become and trying to hide the changes from the world. If the character is a woman, her transformation will often be linked with her menstrual cycle, both being monthly changes that society considers taboo. Ginger Snaps (2000) and Teen Wolf (1985) are two of the more popular examples of this metaphor.
Though these are certainly not the only metaphors that exist for werewolves in media, these two are the basis of the Werewolf aesthetic.

The color palette of the Werewolf aesthetic is pretty neutral -- black, gray, and brown are the basis, with red, blue, and purple being common additions. Typical visuals include the moon (usually a full moon), foggy nights, wolves and dogs, sharp bared teeth, blood, raw meat, animal bones, and forests. More modern depictions will also have them using motorcycles, wearing ripped or patchwork clothing, having tattoos, and long fingernails.

Like the Vampire, the fashion for the Werewolf aesthetic tends to be alternative in nature, though rarely ever fully Goth. Werewolves are depicted as hot-headed hotties who live by their own rules and never deny their true inner nature. This manifests as Werewolf characters adhering to a typical 90s Cool "bad boy" aesthetic, even if they're a woman. Leather jackets and gloves, long dusters, flannels, and combat boots are common here. Their clothes are often ripped or bloodstained, possibly due to being worn during a transformation or fight. They are also tied closely to animal prints and fur of any kind, a hint to their animalistic nature. Male werewolves often opt for jeans, a t-shirt, and a jacket -- sometimes a flannel. Female werewolves dress similarly, but can also dress up the look with a midi skirt and knee-high boots, or possibly even a fur-lined coat. Sometimes the Werewolf will also have bleached or dyed hair, or oddly-colored eyes.
Dark-wash and black jeans, usually distressed/destroyed
Crosses, moons, animal bones, and gemstones as necklace pendants
